summary: A web app that checks whether a trend in NASA Data is real. It disambiguates possible trends from real trends, identifying which are significant. Each answer is graded as robust, likely, not yet detectable, or suspect. It also highlights and classifies contradictions between source data as explained, with explanations, or unexplainable.
details:
Earth System Trend Detective answers one question about NASA Earth data: is this trend real? You type something like "is the Arctic warming?" and the app picks the dataset and region, then shows the monthly series, a trend map and every test it ran.

Each trend goes through five steps: a naive test, the seasonal cycle removed, autocorrelation, a test against every other pixel on the map, and a check against an independent dataset. Any step can be switched off to see what a plain test would have claimed. The answer is graded Robust, Likely, Not yet detectable or Suspect, with the reason written out. Robust needs agreement from a second dataset that shares no input with the first. Suspect means the trend lines up with a dated change in how the data were made, such as the 2006 rain-gauge switch behind MERRA-2 rainfall over the Amazon. The app keeps a catalogue of these changes, each with a source.

Significance comes from 2,000 simulated trend-free series with the same autocorrelation as the data. On simulated series with no trend and white or AR(1) noise, every test used in a verdict flags between 3 % and 8 % at the 5 % level; a plain t-test flags about 40 % when month-to-month autocorrelation is 0.7. Map pixels use the seasonal Mann-Kendall test with false-discovery control.

The app also compares NASA datasets that measure the same thing. It tests the trend of their difference over the cells and months both cover, and calls a gap unexplained only when no catalogued dataset change or measurement limit accounts for it. Of 212 pair-and-region tests, 22 are unexplained. Eight of these are MERRA-2 against the GISTEMP weather stations, and MERRA-2 warms less in all eight. Over the Arctic it is 0.38 against 0.70 °C per decade since 1981, a gap of 0.33 that reaches 0.54 in December–February. Each entry says where the gap is, when it opened and what was ruled out, so the teams behind the datasets can check it.

A scan runs the same tests on 17 variables over 27 named regions and the trend regions on each map, 603 tests in all. Results export as CSV, images, share links, a methods paragraph with citations, and a read-only API.

The system is creative because it unifies the entire problem into a single solution. It also allows users to draw region selections on the globe and see the trend within their selection. Another creative step taken was to highlight conflicts between datasets and classify them as Explained, with the explanation, or Unexplained. Unexplained conflicts may be of interest to the user.

The system does have some known limits I have accepted. The station record covers about 41 % of the globe, so over the oceans there is no independent check of air temperature. Series with long memory are a weak spot, and a trend that fails the long-memory test is capped at Likely. The discrepancy rules don't yet catch every known cause. The question box matches keywords, it is not a language model.


Built with Python (xarray, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, FastAPI) and TypeScript (d3, Vite). I use Claude Code for the code.
